passage: Everyone in my class thought I was being dramatic when I rolled my eyes at the new rule. The school had banned phones in the canteen and started handing out detention slips, and nobody asked us. I sighed loudly every recess for a week. I stopped eating with the girls and stared out of the window. My friend Farida said, "You're just being a brat." That hurt more than the rule. Later I understood I wasn't angry at the rule as much as at not being heard. So I wrote a polite letter with three reasons and twenty signatures and gave it to the principal. She didn't cancel the rule, but she agreed to meet a student group. Deepika.

qa.q: What did the school ban in the canteen?
qa.a: The school banned phones in the canteen.

qa.q: What was Deepika really upset about besides the rule?
qa.a: Deepika realised the anger was mostly about nobody asking the students, and the real wish was to be heard and respected. The sighing and silence hid that wish.

qa.q: What did Deepika do that worked better than sighing?
qa.a: Deepika wrote a polite letter with reasons and signatures and gave it to the principal, who agreed to meet a student group.

qa.q: How might Farida have seen Deepika's eye-rolls?
qa.a: Farida may have seen them as sulking or attitude, without seeing what was underneath. 🙂

grounding: A teen protests a rule with eye-rolls and sighs, and a respectful channel gets a hearing.

passage: Coach's note, Thursday. Dolma led about fifteen students to the gate at lunch with a hand-lettered sign: 'Keep the library open till 6.' They stood quietly on the side without blocking anyone. Some rolled their eyes and sighed at the staff, and one boy got loud. Dolma pulled him aside and reminded him about their plan. I watched from the pitch. I wondered if the protest was about the library hours or about wanting to be listened to, and her face suggested a bit of both. I asked her to send her request in writing to the principal, and I offered to attach my support. She said, "Thank you, sir." Sahil, sports coach.

qa.a: Her sign said, 'Keep the library open till 6.'

qa.q: What might Dolma be feeling and wanting behind the protest?
qa.a: She seems to want the library to stay open and to have students' voices heard, and Sahil thinks it may be a bit of both. She also acted responsibly by calming the loud boy.

qa.q: What could Dolma do next to make the protest effective?
qa.a: Send a written request to the principal with the coach's support and keep the group peaceful and respectful.

qa.q: How might a teacher watching the gate feel about the protest?
qa.a: They may feel challenged or worried about disruption, or they may respect the calm way the students went about it.

grounding: A teen joins a peaceful protest, and respectful channels are more effective than escalation.
